name: History of Foreign Trade
description: Iran’s foreign trade has connected regional producers and merchants with markets across Eurasia and the Indian Ocean. From early modern silk commerce to state-regulated imports and contemporary regional trading relationships, its history reveals changing connections between commerce, political power, and international access.

seo.title: History of Foreign Trade in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iranian foreign trade from early modern merchant networks to state regulation, regional markets, and verified EU goods-trade data.

content.heading: Networks across land and sea
content.content:
Iran’s early modern commerce operated through overlapping land and maritime networks. Under the Safavids, the dynasty that ruled from the beginning of the sixteenth century, merchants traded with Ottoman territories, India, Russia, and Central Asia. European trading companies added another layer to these relationships. Maritime commerce through the Persian Gulf expanded substantially, but overland exchange continued: one route did not simply replace another. [s1](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/commerce-vi/)

Silk was a prominent export, alongside products including horses, goat hair, and pearls. Imports included textiles, spices, metals, and sugar. Armenian merchants became important participants in the silk business, connecting production with markets abroad. Commerce also depended on arrangements with rulers, customs officials, brokers, and shipping companies. Shah Abbas I’s silk-export monopoly illustrates how a government could intervene directly in a valuable commodity rather than merely tax its movement. [s1](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/commerce-vi/)

The surviving evidence is uneven. European company archives illuminate particular transactions, but their share of total Iranian commerce is uncertain. They cannot establish a complete national trade balance for the early modern period. [s1](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/commerce-vi/)

content.heading: From merchant commerce to administrative control
content.content:
Before the Pahlavi monarchy, foreign merchants operated under treaty protections, while Iranian merchants also served as agents for overseas firms. These overlapping roles make a simple division between domestic and foreign commercial activity misleading. During the Pahlavi period, government intervention expanded through import restrictions, commodity quotas, and state trading companies. Export certificates linked permission to import with prior export activity, making administrative access part of a merchant’s business. [s2](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/commerce-vii/)

Commercial decision-making also became more concentrated in Tehran. Transport connections, government offices, and state monopoly companies drew activity toward the capital, reducing the relative autonomy of provincial trading centers. This geographical shift helps explain why the history of foreign trade belongs to the history of Iranian cities as well as international relations. [s2](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/commerce-vii/)

After the revolution and during the war with Iraq, administrative controls sharply restricted private importing. Nowshirvani’s historical account distinguishes constitutional provisions and proposed legislation from the administrative measures actually used. It describes the expansion of government and foundation participation; it should not be read as a description of today’s legal arrangements. [s2](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/commerce-vii/)

content.heading: A changing export basket
content.content:
The WTO’s inspected country profile identifies China, Iraq, the United Arab Emirates, and Türkiye among the principal destinations in its reported export data. Its product listings include liquefied hydrocarbons, methanol, bitumen, fertilizer, plastics, and steel. This is a substantially different commercial landscape from one organized around silk and caravan routes, although neighboring markets remain important. The same profile explicitly identifies Iran as a non-member of the WTO. [s3](https://ttd.wto.org/en/profiles/iran)

These listings require care: the profile attributes its trade figures to Trade Data Monitor, and this page does not treat them as a verified measure of every Iranian export channel. Nor does a recorded trading partner necessarily identify the final consumer of goods moving through an intermediary economy. The profile provides a documented snapshot, rather than a complete account of the mechanisms behind each transaction. [s3](https://ttd.wto.org/en/profiles/iran)

content.heading: One measurable relationship
content.content:
The chart isolates EU-reported goods imports from Iran. The series rises to its highest displayed level in 2017, falls sharply in 2019, and remains below that earlier peak through 2025. It measures nominal value, so it cannot by itself distinguish changes in prices, physical quantities, or product composition. It also cannot establish the causes of the decline. [s4](https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/isdb_results/factsheets/country/details_iran_en.pdf)

Reading trade history therefore requires two questions together: what moved across borders, and which institutions recorded or controlled that movement? Merchant archives, historical customs reports, and contemporary partner statistics answer different parts of that question. [s1](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/commerce-vi/) [s2](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/commerce-vii/) [s4](https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/isdb_results/factsheets/country/details_iran_en.pdf)

name: Social History
description: Iran’s social history examines how people organized households, livelihoods, settlements, and access to learning across changing political and economic conditions. It connects urban, rural, and nomadic experiences while recognizing substantial differences between regions, social groups, and generations.

seo.title: Iranian Social History: Families, Settlements and Learning | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Discover the connected histories of Iranian villages, cities, pastoral communities, families, education, and internal migration.

content.heading: History at the scale of everyday life
content.content: A change of dynasty does not tell us, by itself, how a household earned a living, who controlled a harvest, or how children learned to read. Social history follows these relationships across political turning points. In Iran, it must also connect distinct settings: villages organized around cultivation, mobile pastoral communities using seasonal grazing, and households whose responsibilities changed alongside wage employment and public services. These settings were interconnected rather than successive stages through which everyone passed. [s1](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/deh/) [s2](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/nomadism/) [s3](https://www.persee.fr/doc/pop_1634-2941_2002_num_57_2_18397)

content.heading: Villages were not all alike
content.content:
The Persian term deh denotes a village understood as a social and spatial unit. Its physical form varied with ecology and local history. On arid foothill plains, clustered settlements often developed around irrigation channels or qanats, underground galleries that convey groundwater. Water access could reflect differences in wealth and influence within the settlement. In the humid Caspian provinces of Gilan and Mazandaran, dispersed farmsteads created a markedly different landscape. [s1](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/deh/)

Settlement patterns could also preserve histories of mobility. Some communities originating in pastoral groups combined a permanent village with temporary camps or complementary agricultural land. A house, therefore, does not prove that seasonal movement had ended. This regional variety makes any single picture of the timeless Iranian village inadequate. [s1](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/deh/)

content.heading: Landownership was a social relationship
content.content:
Amlak, privately owned agricultural estates, could encompass several villages. Their administration linked landowners, estate managers, village headmen, and cultivators. Sharecropping distributed agricultural output according to contributions that could include land, water, seed, animals, and labor. Ownership consequently affected authority and dependence as well as income. [s4](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/amlak/)

Absentee ownership further complicates a sharp division between countryside and city: an estate owner might live in town while a manager supervised production. The land reform implemented during the Pahlavi period challenged this system of large estates. Its significance was social as well as agricultural, because it altered established relationships between cultivators and those who controlled village resources. The history of rural life therefore requires attention to power and unequal access, alongside crops and architecture. [s4](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/amlak/)

content.heading: Mobility as an organized livelihood
content.content:
Pastoral nomadism involved regular movement along known routes between grazing areas. In Iran’s mountain environments, summer uplands and winter lowlands offered complementary resources. Such movement was an organized response to seasonality, not aimless wandering. Herds linked households to landscapes unsuitable for continuous cultivation. [s2](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/nomadism/)

Government settlement policies, pressure on grazing areas, schooling, and integration into wider markets changed pastoral life. These developments did not produce one uniform outcome: continued migration, partial settlement, and changing combinations of occupations all belong to the history. It is therefore essential to distinguish tribal affiliation, which concerns social identity and organization, from the actual practice of moving livestock and households. [s2](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/nomadism/)

content.heading: Households, kinship, and public services
content.content:
Historian and demographer Marie Ladier-Fouladi describes the family as historically providing much more than domestic companionship: kin could help secure work, arrange marriage, support education, and care for older relatives. Her study connects changes in these functions with wage labor, urbanization, and access to state-funded services. This is an interpretation of social transformation, rather than proof that extended kinship simply disappeared. [s3](https://www.persee.fr/doc/pop_1634-2941_2002_num_57_2_18397)

The distinction between a family and a household matters. A census household records a residential arrangement; relationships of support can extend beyond it. Ladier-Fouladi also identifies limitations in older census categories and fragmentary surveys. A smaller household should therefore not automatically be interpreted as weaker family ties or greater personal autonomy. [s3](https://www.persee.fr/doc/pop_1634-2941_2002_num_57_2_18397)

content.heading: Learning and the uneven reach of change
content.content:
Education connects these histories because access to learning depends on where people live, their work, and their family circumstances. UNESCO’s account of a literacy and computer-skills initiative recognized in 2018 describes the Literacy Movement Organization’s attention to women and girls in rural areas and other underserved groups. It documents a particular program and its stated priorities; an award does not establish that educational inequality was eliminated. [s5](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/unesco-literacy-prize-awarded-project-iran-promoting-literacy-and-computer-skills)

The branches below pursue these distinctions separately. Urbanization concerns the changing distribution and organization of settlement; migration concerns movement between places; family history examines relationships that may persist across both. Read together with rural and nomadic histories, they show why social change should be investigated through specific institutions and experiences rather than described as a single national journey from tradition to modernity. [s1](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/deh/) [s2](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/nomadism/) [s3](https://www.persee.fr/doc/pop_1634-2941_2002_num_57_2_18397)

name: History of Urbanization
description: Iran’s urbanization history joins long-established cities with modern changes in planning, industry, housing, and population distribution. Annual international estimates show a rising urban population share, but that measure must be distinguished from migration, built-up expansion, and changes in settlement classification.

seo.title: History of Urbanization in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Trace Iranian city growth through historic neighborhoods, modern planning, industrialization, and annual urban-share estimates for 2012–2025.

content.heading: Cities before mass urbanization
content.content:
Modern urbanization transformed places that already had distinctive urban institutions. Eckart Ehlers describes a recurring historical pattern organized around a bazaar, residential quarters, and facilities for commerce. A bazaar was both a marketplace and a concentration of commercial and craft activity; a mahalla was a neighborhood with its own local facilities. This is a useful model, but Ehlers also acknowledges criticism of treating Middle Eastern cities as one uniform type. [s1](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/cities-iv/)

Yazd offers a concrete example of adaptation to an arid environment. UNESCO describes districts associated with qanats, underground water-conveyance systems, and houses using courtyards, thick earthen walls, and windcatchers. Its historic fabric includes commercial, communal, and residential spaces. Urban history here concerns the coordination of water, buildings, and neighborhood life, rather than the growth of population alone. [s2](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1544/)

content.heading: New streets and new centers
content.content:
Under Reza Shah, modernizing interventions superimposed avenues and new street patterns on older urban cores. Centrally directed designs introduced comparable public spaces and building forms in different cities. Expansion also involved movement within cities: prosperous residents could finance and occupy new districts while older houses accommodated incoming residents. This helps explain why urban transformation cannot be reduced to migration from villages. [s1](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/cities-iv/)

Industrialization created another route to urban growth. Isfahan’s historical geography connects its modern development with textile production and later heavy industry. The steel complex established with Soviet assistance drew on water, energy access, and an existing skilled workforce. Its location demonstrates how state investment could reshape an established city’s economic role. The same historical account identifies migration from nearby mountain regions and wartime movement from Khuzestan as contributors to the city’s demographic growth. [s3](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/isfahan-ii-historical-geography/)

content.heading: What the urban share measures
content.content:
The World Bank indicator used below follows national statistical definitions of urban residence and incorporates United Nations Population Division smoothing. It measures the proportion of people classified as urban, rather than the area covered by buildings. Differences in administrative boundaries and settlement definitions therefore matter. A rising share is not, by itself, a count of people who moved from countryside to city. [s4](https://databank.worldbank.org/metadataglossary/world-development-indicators/series/SP.URB.TOTL.IN.ZS)

The inspected annual values increase throughout the displayed period. They are retained as source-produced estimates, not presented as independent census observations for every year. The missing final year preserves the distinction between a research cutoff and an available reporting year. [s5](https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/IRN/indicator/SP.URB.TOTL.IN.ZS?format=json)

content.y_axis_label: Urban residents as percent of total population, 0–100

content.title: Different routes to a changing urban population
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["Movement between settlements"] -->|"Can change residence totals"| D["Population recorded in urban areas"]
  B["Population change within settlements"] -->|"Can change resident totals"| D
  C["Urban definitions and boundaries"] -->|"Determine classification"| D
  D -->|"Numerator"| E["Urban share of national population"]
  F["Total national population"] -->|"Denominator"| E
```
content.summary: The diagram separates population processes from classification. It does not quantify their individual contributions or imply that the annual series measures migration directly.

content.heading: Growth and continuity
content.content:
Modernization did not erase every older urban system. UNESCO’s assessment of Yazd describes an inhabited historic city where traditional buildings have also acquired educational, hospitality, and other uses. Its account notes that much modern development occurred outside the historic fabric. Conservation and urban change can therefore coexist, although a heritage assessment should not be mistaken for a complete evaluation of contemporary housing conditions. [s2](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1544/)

Reading Iran’s urban past requires both scales: national population evidence and the histories of particular places. A national trend can establish the direction of change; neighborhoods, industrial districts, and water systems explain how that change took physical and social form. [s2](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1544/) [s3](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/isfahan-ii-historical-geography/) [s4](https://databank.worldbank.org/metadataglossary/world-development-indicators/series/SP.URB.TOTL.IN.ZS)
